summary: Surveys transport protocols designed to take less bandwidth, or add less delay, than standard TCP when sharing a bottleneck with it. Such lower-than-best-effort protocols suit delay-insensitive background traffic, like bulk transfers that should not slow down interactive use.

plainLanguage.summary: Some downloads should be polite and let important traffic go first, like a car pulling over for an ambulance. This paper lists the different ways people have designed internet traffic to be that polite.

questions: lower than best effort transport protocols
subtitle: Transport protocols designed to be polite to other traffic

tldr.problem: When background traffic like bulk downloads shares a network with interactive or high-priority traffic, it can significantly slow down the important applications. Standard TCP is aggressive and does not yield easily to other flows.
tldr.mechanism: Lower-than-best-effort (LBE) protocols reduce their sending rate more aggressively than standard TCP when they detect congestion or other flows, allowing them to minimize interference with foreground traffic while still using available spare capacity.
tldr.outcome: The survey describes several approaches: delay-based protocols that slow down when latency increases, loss-based protocols that accept a smaller share of bandwidth, application-layer techniques, and network-assisted mechanisms using routers. The LEDBAT working group standardized a delay-based algorithm for this purpose.

today: RFC 6297 is an Informational document describing a landscape of LBE protocols and approaches. LEDBAT was standardized as a congestion control algorithm, but widespread deployment remains limited. In practice, a mix of transport-layer, application-layer, and network-layer techniques are used to manage background traffic in production networks.

sections.title: Background Traffic and Congestion
sections.content:
Lower-than-best-effort (LBE) protocols are designed to have a smaller bandwidth and delay impact on standard TCP when both share a bottleneck. An LBE service is useful for delay-insensitive background traffic like large file transfers that should not interfere with interactive applications or real-time services.

The core challenge is that standard TCP, once started, ramps up its sending rate until it fills the available bandwidth and causes packets to drop. When a standard TCP flow competes with other traffic, it gets its fair share but does not willingly yield to higher-priority applications. An LBE protocol must react to congestion signals earlier than standard TCP or accept a smaller share of the bandwidth, allowing it to back off before high-priority traffic suffers.

This survey covers multiple categories of approaches: delay-based transport protocols that detect congestion from increases in round-trip time, loss-based protocols that adjust their rate based on packet loss, application-layer techniques that do not require changes to the transport protocol itself, and network-assisted approaches that rely on support from routers or the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal downloads are a bit greedy: they use as much bandwidth as possible, which can make web pages slow to load. The idea is to make bulk downloads voluntarily use less bandwidth when someone is trying to do something interactive on the network.

sections.title: Delay-Based Protocols
sections.content:
Delay-based protocols detect congestion by measuring round-trip time (RTT) and react when the RTT increases, which signals that packets are queuing up in buffers. The idea is to slow down before packets drop, unlike standard TCP which reacts only after loss occurs.

TCP Vegas, one of the earliest examples, measures the difference between expected and actual throughput and adjusts its sending rate based on RTT changes. It calculates expected throughput as the congestion window divided by the baseline (minimum) RTT and compares this to actual throughput derived from acknowledgments. If actual throughput is less than expected, the sender linearly decreases its rate. If it is greater than a lower threshold (alpha), the sender increases its rate.

TCP Nice improves on Vegas by avoiding excessive linear rate decreases that can affect standard TCP flows. Instead of linearly reducing the window, TCP Nice halves the congestion window (at most once per RTT) only if a fixed fraction of delay-based congestion signals appear within one RTT. This makes it less intrusive to competing standard TCP flows.

TCP-LP and Sync-TCP use one-way delay instead of round-trip time to avoid reacting to reverse-path congestion. TCP-LP monitors the exponentially weighted moving average of one-way delay and halves its window when delay exceeds a threshold, then waits an additional RTT to confirm persistent congestion before reducing to one packet per RTT.

The advantage of delay-based approaches is that they react to congestion signals before packets drop. The disadvantage is that delay measurements are noisy, affected by factors like buffering variability, reverse-path congestion, wireless effects, and processing delays in hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: When your computer notices the network is getting slower (ping time increases), it voluntarily slows down its downloads so interactive traffic doesn't get stuck in a queue. It's like pulling over when you see traffic ahead, before the road gets completely jammed.

sections.title: Other Transport and Application Approaches
sections.content:
Non-delay-based protocols take a different approach. 4CP (Competitive and Considerate Congestion Control) maintains a virtual window that is reduced below a minimum value during "bad congestion" phases. Whether congestion is "good" or "bad" depends on the loss event rate. MulTFRC extends TCP-Friendly Rate Control to support fractional emulation of N parallel TCP flows, allowing N between 0 and 1 to achieve lower-than-best-effort behavior.

Application-layer approaches do not require modifying transport protocols. BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service), used in Microsoft Windows, applies application-level priority levels and monitors network bandwidth usage so low-priority transfers yield to high-priority ones. Receiver-window tuning exploits TCP's flow control mechanism: a receiver can manipulate its advertised window size to control the sender's rate, allowing the receiver to enforce rate limits without changing TCP itself.

Network-assisted approaches leverage router support. Harp uses multipath routing to steer background traffic to less-utilized paths. NF-TCP (Network-Friendly TCP) uses explicit congestion notification (ECN) and active queue management (AQM) to mark low-priority packets with higher probability than high-priority ones, allowing the network to signal congestion to background flows.
sections.plainLanguage: If delay-based detection sounds too tricky, there are other ways: applications can ask for a smaller piece of the bandwidth, receivers can ask senders to slow down, or routers can mark packets with a priority level so bulk transfers know when to back off.

sections.title: The LEDBAT Algorithm and Deployment
sections.content:
The LEDBAT (Low Extra Delay Background Transport) working group standardized a delay-based congestion control algorithm designed specifically for background traffic. LEDBAT is classified as a delay-based mechanism similar to protocols described above, relying heavily on RTT to detect incipient congestion.

However, LEDBAT is an algorithm, not a protocol specification; how it is actually deployed in the internet (which transport protocols use it, how signaling works) was left to other work. Because LEDBAT relies on delay, the accuracy issues discussed in the delay-based section apply to it. Research comparing LEDBAT with other approaches (like TCP-LP, TCP Nice, and traditional TCP) shows performance improvements but requires careful interpretation, as LEDBAT specifications were still evolving at the time of these analyses.

The choice of approach depends on deployment constraints. Delay-based and loss-based transport protocols require changes to endpoints' TCP implementations. Application-layer techniques are easier to deploy because they work with existing transport protocols but may be limited in applicability. Network-assisted approaches offer better protection of non-LBE flows but require modifications to intermediate network nodes, which complicates deployment.

In practice, many networks use a combination: delay-based congestion control at the transport layer, application-level priority management, and network-level quality-of-service mechanisms working together to protect high-priority traffic while allowing background transfers to use spare capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF standardized a delay-based algorithm called LEDBAT that tries to be polite to other traffic. But the algorithm alone doesn't solve everything: endpoints, applications, and networks all have to cooperate to make background traffic truly low-priority.
